newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Quiet, range-bound trade seen.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Quiet, range-bound trade seen.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were expected to remain in narrow trading ranges Wednesday as market participants awaited further readings on the strength of the economy.

Due out Wednesday was the Federal Reserve's Beige Book, an account of business conditions around the nation based on anecdotal observations in the Fed's 12 districts. Traditionally, the report has not been a market-mover.
February retail sales were due Thursday and February producer prices and industrial production were set for Friday.

Dallas Fed president Robert McTeer told a newswire on Tuesday that labor markets were tight and the danger of wage pressures exceeding productivity growth existed. He said the Fed was on guard but there was not enough evidence of higher prices to tip policymakers into tightening. Those comments helped cheer an otherwise listless market.

John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co., characterized McTeer's comments as "ridiculous" and said any gain the market realized from them probably would be short-lived. The market has too many potential negatives weighing on it at the current time, he said.
"McTeer is not a voting member of the FOMC and, more importantly, he's not Alan Greenspan. I doubt McTeer meant to prejudge Greenspan's call," Williams said.

Williams said the Beige Book could provide anecdotal evidence of wage pressures, retail sales were expected to be strong on Thursday and initial weekly jobless claims could once again evince a tight labor market. Industrial production also has the potential of unnerving the market, he said.
A Reuters poll of 44 Wall Street economists on Monday showed 17 forecast a rate hike in March, with 34 predicting a tightening by the Fed's subsequent meeting, May 20.

"I'm not sure I believe Greenspan when he says he's going to be preemptive," Williams said. "The justification is there for the Fed to move at any time, the only question is when and that's not exactly clear."
Williams said when the Fed had solid inflationary statistics it would hike rates 25 basis points and another 25 basis points at a subsequent meeting.

"Tomorrow the big release is the Beige Book and with the market scrutinizing everything it can its reading of the Beige Book will be important," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.
With the market as skittish as it currently is, players will pay attention to how much the Beige Book mentions wage pressures and its emphasis on economic growth in recent months, Kretzmer said.
"The bias right now is a worried bias that maybe a tightening has still not been fully priced in," Kretzmer said.
However, given the dearth of economic data with which to trade on, Kretzmer said he expected any movement up or down not to exceed one-half a point on Wednesday.
"In front of retail sales on Thursday, we won't see a lot of movement, he said.

Late Tuesday afternoon three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.04 percent. Six-month bill rates were down one basis point at 5.17 percent. Year bill rates were down two basis points at 5.36 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 at 99-20/32, yielding 6.08 percent. Five-year notes were down 1/32 at 99-12/32, yielding 6.40 percent. Ten-year notes were down 3/32 to 97-24/32, yielding 6.56 percent.
The 30-year bond was trading off 09/32 at 97-8/32 to yield 6.84 percent.
